div.head: Hn 9.4a
div.ab: Transeunt autem multis modis, alia intrinsecis alia extrinsecis accidenciis, secundum industriam uel insciciam concausancium, secundum socam prelatorum, quam quidam habent in suo de suis, quidam de suis et extraneis, siue in omnibus siue in quibusdam causis.

Übertragung des Prozesses an anderes Gericht vermutet Maitland Domesday 292 schon in Mercischen Urkk. 9. Jhs. hinter dem Worte vicissitudo, das ich aber = vicis ‘Mal’ übersetze.—Vielleicht ist der ‘äussere Umstand’ hier die Zuständigkeit der privaten Gerichtsbarkeit (s. d. Gl 37 ff.), der ‘innere’ das Benehmen der Parteien im Prozess.—multis a. intrincecis{20} a. extrincecis ohne modis—causancium{22} Rs

Maitland (Domesday 292) suspects the transfer of a case to another court already in Mercian charters of the 9th cent., behind the word vicissitudo, which, however, I translate = vicis ‘time, occasion’.—Perhaps the ‘external circumstance’ here is the competence of private jurisdiction (see that word in Gl 37 ff.), the ‘internal’ one the conduct of the parties in the suit.—multis a. intrincecis{20} a. extrincecis without modis—causancium{22} Rs

div.ab: They pass, however, in many ways, some by intrinsic, some by extrinsic accidents, according to the diligence or ignorance of the parties, according to the soke of the lords, which some have on their own land over their own men, some over their own men and strangers, whether in all or in certain cases.
